I can tell you that of all the students who have gone and will go through Laval university, none so far has ever shown and probably will never show such legal comprehension as he. I consider him a genius in the field of law and I think he will go far." Such an appraisal becomes even more eloquent and valuable since it came from a man who, apart from being level-headed, harboured political ideas different from his clerk's.
That prophetic utterance was true. It was confirmed when this man, whom we admire so much and who has been so gifted in the choice of his colleagues in the various fields of political activity in the country, was unanimously chosen by all the provinces as their leader.
Why did I make that profession of faith? Well, because I have been a Liberal for fifty years, because I have always supported the Liberal party and advocated Liberal principles, my constituents did not much relish the word "independent" coupled with my name by some newspapers. I did not particularly like being called by that unwarranted term. I hope I will not have to uphold my own political party for another fifty years before I can prove that I am a Liberal.
Some local papers even went so far as to say that I was in disgrace in this house. As far as I am concerned I never did take offence at being given a seat in one particular section of the house, because I think that a member's political beliefs retain their strength whether he sits close to or far from the government benches. Mr. Speaker, the Liberal electrical current which has always held me to my party was as strong from my seat over there as if I had sat next to the Prime Minister and his colleagues of the cabinet. An alternating current is as strong at the end of a line as it is when it comes out of the generator.
I am now here through the explicit and formal wish of the electors of Rimouski county; they have asked me, by a substantial majority, to take the place of the late Mr. Gleason Belzile, who had represented the riding so worthily since 1945.

The Budget-Mr. Rousseau
The designs of Providence are inscrutable. Mr. Belzile, who enjoyed the affection of his family and the admiration of his party, was carried off at a time when he was constantly earning new laurels.
The fine gentlemanly qualities, the seriousness and the competence of my distinguished and lamented predecessor had been noticed by his superiors. He had already attained the important office of parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), the nation's tireless and distinguished treasurer.
I remember what the Prime Minister said when he visited our constituency in 1949, accompanied by his charming wife, Mrs. St. Laurent. I quote: "Ladies and gentlemen, I ask you to elect Gleason Belzile; we need him in Ottawa. He has already attained a high position, but we want him to go much higher."
In answer to that call, I, who now have the honour and pleasure of speaking to you, did all in my power, and went all out, if I may use a popular phrase, to ensure Mr. Belzile's victory.
What I did in 1949 was done at the special request of our distinguished Prime Minister and to make up for the inertia evident in others. Judging by the flattering letter he wrote to me after the election, we must have succeeded remarkably well.
May I, Mr. Speaker, be permitted to interject in this profession of faith in the Liberal doctrine my own patriotic profession of faith: five of my sons were on active service during the last war, four of them overseas and one of them in Canada. The one who married Miss Belzile spent three and a half years as a prisoner in Germany. He was an observer in the R.A.F.; eight days before he was brought down over Hamburg, the King had honoured him by chatting with him in French for almost half an hour when my son, the only French-speaking Canadian member of his squadron, told him he came from Canada.
Let me say also that the last honours paid by the province of Quebec to Their Majesties the King and Queen were paid at Trois Pistoles by the person who has the privilege of addressing you at this moment. The mounted police had asked me to prepare vocal and band music to salute Their Majesties when the royal train made a stop at Trois Pistoles during the night, to replenish its water supply. At the time, I

had seventy-five youngsters, accompanied by the band I have been conducting for 50 years, sing God Save the King, O Canada, and Alouette for the Queen.
Personally, during both world wars, I prevented an act of sabotage which might have had most harmful effects on Canada's war effort. Let me explain.
At Trois Pistoles, there is a high bridge on the C.N.R. line. When, during the first world war, German submarine activity was preventing the sending of American soldiers to Europe through New York, American troops took the C.N.R. to Halifax. One day, to the west of the village, there settled a man who claimed to be a veterinary surgeon. I was rather dubious about the real reason for his stay. I thought that this stranger had some other idea in his mind than just looking after sick animals. I took him for a spy entrusted with the job of blowing up the railway bridge.
I then came to Ottawa, at my own expense, in order to acquaint the authorities with my misgivings. Sir Eugene Fiset, a personal friend of mine, was at the time deputy minister of militia. The session was on and parliament sat in the national museum, the parliament buildings having burnt down. Sir Eugene then introduced me to the Hon. Sam Hughes, to whom I communicated my misgivings, and a few weeks later the stranger disappeared.
One Sunday afternoon, during the last war, I dislodged from under the same bridge a stranger who had settled there with his easel and paint brushes to paint the bridge. I immediately notified the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and, a few hours later, the intruder had been shooed away and the bridge was left standing.
Before giving you, Mr. Speaker, as true a description as possible of my county to make it better known, I have a very pleasant duty to perform, in the name of my electors as well as in my own name, towards the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois).
During the long and painful illness of the late Mr. Belzile, the hon. member agreed to look after the interests of Rimouski county as well as those of his own constituency. It was a heavy task and he did a wonderful job. I might even add that it has affected his health. For that hard and tiring work, I offer him once more my thanks and those of my electors.
As I do not wish to impose upon his kindness, and knowing besides that his new duties as parliamentary assistant to the Postmaster General mean more work for him, I am willing to look after all the work pertaining

to my county. However, I shall still be asking for his help and his advice, and I know that he will give me both.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am proud to tell you about my county, 312 square miles in area, with a population of over 61,000, including nearly 30,000 electors.
Between Trois Pistoles, its western boundary, and Mont Joli, its eastern boundary, the distance is 60 miles facing the beautiful St. Lawrence river, the average width of which, at this point, is 35 miles.
As the waters of the river begin to get salty at L'Islet, 150 miles farther west, it is really salty at that point of the St. Lawrence river. My county extends 52 miles to the south.
This area of 312 square miles comprises 34 well-organized parishes, 34 churches, 25 convents, 1 classical college, 1 seminary and 1 bishopric.
This reminds me that last fall, the Rimouski diocese mourned the loss of its archbishop, the Most Rev. Courchesne. He passed away in November. In March, Rome appointed her new representative, Most Rev. Parent whose school examinations I had the honour to supervise when he was six years old.
A few hours after he had been appointed, I went to Rimouski to offer him my respects on my own behalf and on behalf of my electors. He then recalled having met the Speaker of the House of Commons in Rome during the summer. He urged me to offer him his regards, which I am most glad to do.
Now, if I may continue: 1 school of agriculture, 1 technical school, 1 school of commerce, 1 navy school, 4 commercial schools. There are 210 male teachers, 7 female teachers, 141 schools and 6,271 children attending those elementary schools. We have a hospital, a sanatorium, two newspapers, three homes for the aged. There are 3,500 farmers, 697 settlers, 2,459 day-labourers. There are also 342 farm tractors, 11 butter factories, 9 cheese factories, 80 industries, 10 tinsmiths, 22 shoemakers, 23 blacksmiths, 205 merchants, 36 hotels, 114 professional men-doctors, notaries, lawyers, surveyors, agronomists-and 73 restaurants.
Although I have represented Rimouski for the past six months only, I have tried to be well informed in order to give immediate answers to the legitimate and reasonable
The Budget-Mr. Rousseau requests of my constituents. Mr. Speaker, if I may judge from the hundreds of letters I have received since I was elected, I am considered by all the electors as their representative with the government. My electors and myself are convinced that the present Liberal government will be pleased to consider the requests submitted by the representative elected by the majority.
On the St. Lawrence, there are three cities, Trois Pistoles to the west, Mont Joli to the east, and Rimouski practically in the centre. Mont Joli takes its name from its beautiful, lofty site; a little to the west, on a great height there is the St. Georges sanatorium, an impressive building accommodating nearly 600 patients who receive remarkable care and attention from the religious authorities, the director, nurses, doctors, attendants and the whole staff. I had the opportunity to visit this fine institution and I was truly amazed by the splendid work accomplished there for the recovery of our dear patients.
I know the Department of National Health and Welfare has paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward this hospital. I understand there will be other requirements and I know my requests will be well received by the minister of health when I submit them.
The railway terminal and divisional point of the C.N.R. are located at Mont Joli. A good many of its citizens are railroad employees, still on the payroll or retired.
I know that a large number of the retired employees will ask the government, if they have not already done so, for an increase in pension. Their request is justified and I shall consider it a duty and a pleasure to support their claims.
Yesterday afternoon, in the railways committee, I had the pleasure of learning from Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the board of the C.N.R., that a committee of representatives of the C.N.R., of the Canadian and international union of railroad employees, had been set up. It is already at work revising the pension of all classes of C.N.R. and former Intercolonial Railway pensioners, with a view to granting all of them a pension in keeping with present standards of living. Mr. Gordon is honest, fair and a real businessman. We are confident he will treat everyone fairly.
During the last war, the Department of National Defence built an airport which I know the people of Mont Joli wish to preserve



The Budget-Mr. Rousseau and expand in order to take care of the increasing volume of business that comes from the north shore.
My lamented predecessor, Mr. Belzile, had succeeded in preventing several buildings from being torn down, even though some people hoped to do away with them. He had even obtained funds for improvements. I am determined that this work will continue, perhaps on an even larger scale, and I am confident that the Minister of National Defence will agree to my request.
A handsome modern building, much of it occupied by the Post Office Department, was inaugurated last September in the centre of Mont Joli.
There is still space available in that building for the staff of an unemployment insurance officer. They could do an excellent job in helping those who have the chance of benefiting from the provisions of this act. There have been urgent requests for the opening of such an office and I hope these requests will be granted in the near future. In the very same building, the people of Mont Joli would like to see and, as a matter of fact, they urgently request the opening of a customs office. Here again, I will take all the necessary steps to have this request given proper consideration.
Mont Joli is also faced with the matter of improving the viaduct in the centre of the town. The municipal authorities have sent me an urgent plea for improvements to this viaduct, now forty years old and no longer meeting the requirements of the people. I will make the necessary representations to the board of transport commissioners in order that they may take the necessary steps to improve this viaduct.
From Mont Joli, Mr. Speaker, you go in a straight line to Ste. Fla vie sur Mer. You will find there a fairly long wharf, which does not seem, however, to ensure adequate protection to the coasting vessels that have to stop there. Should a wharfhead be built in an easterly direction, for a distance of a few hundred feet and thence back landward, you would have there almost a true seaport where these coasters could safely put up, load and discharge cargo even in the heaviest weather.
I have seen that kind of a wharf in New Brunswick. It is of great service to seafaring people. I know that works of that description

would be most useful in that part of my constituency; I intend to request them from the Minister of Public Works. I consider this establishment at Ste. Flavie as being useful to national defence since the coasters transporting war material can easily stop off there.
Leaving Ste. Flavie and going in a westerly direction-always along the river-one comes to Ste. Luce sur Mer, which really rivals "Old Orchard" with its beautiful rockless sandy beach, and its thousands of visitors * during the summer season.
In the fall -and the spring the flood-tide undermines the shore and even the highway.
I understand that the Department of Public Works is going to be asked to build a retaining wall. This matter is also urgent, and I will support that request with all the energy at my command.
Leaving Ste. Luce, again in a westerly direction, and before reaching Rimouski, one comes to Father Point, where the transAtlantic liners pick up or let off the pilots.
I have been told that work has to be done on the wharf at that strategic point. I shall submit the request to the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Transport, as these three departments are interested in that work.
After passing through Rimouski, with which I shall deal further on, we come to Sacre Coeur, an interesting summer resort where real comfort can be found at the Rocher Blanc hotel.
Then you reach Bic. The wharf there needs to be repaired and we shall see to it.
At the entrance to the bay there is a small island on which there is a cave where human bones were discovered a few years ago. According to Relations, a daily record kept by the Jesuit missionaries, it was in this cave that the Iroquois exterminated the last of the Hurons. Before taking refuge in this cave where they thought they would be safe, the Hurons came down the great river-Trois Pistoles river-right to its mouth and had spent three weeks on lie aux Basques. Thinking that the Iroquois had lost their trail, the Hurons came right down to Bic, travelling on the ice, but the Iroquois followed them to the mainland, caught them and exterminated them in this cave.
From Bic we come to St. Fabien, a pretty summer resort, then to St. Simon and to Trois Pistoles.
I will not mention all that could be said of the other parishes in my constituency that do not border the coast; that would be

too long. I can assure you, though, that the people in all of them are most interesting from every point of view. That is where farmers and settlers, especially, are located.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before speaking of the county seat itself, I wish to acquaint you with Trois Pistoles. I will tell you the meaning and the origin of the name. The pistole was a French coin. In the early days of the colony, to go from the village of Trois Pistoles you had to cross a river that the Hurons had called the great river. One day a missionary, crossing that river, tried to draw salt water with a silver goblet. He inadvertently let the goblet fall into the water. Whereupon he told the boatman: "When the tide ebbs, you will find the goblet and keep it as fare." That goblet was worth three pistoles. That true story can be found in the history of Trois Pistoles, written by a member of parliament, the Hon. Charles A. Gauvreau, who married the adopted daughter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and who, for 27 years, ably represented the constituency of Temiscouata in the House of Commons.
For the past 18 years that city has become a sort of smaller Canada. Young men and women from all over Canada come to Trois Pistoles and spend eight weeks there to learn French. When they arrive, from the various English-speaking provinces, they do not speak French at all. Living in families where no English is spoken, they must, of necessity, become familiar with that new language and with the home life of those families. As a result, when they return home after that eight-week course, they speak French fluently. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that these summer courses were inaugurated eighteen years ago by Western university of London, Ontario. At that time, its president was Dr. Sherwood W. Fox, who had dreamed, in his youth, of achieving unity and understanding between the two great races that live in Canada. This patriot always felt that if people were better acquainted, if they could chat together and understand one another, harmonious relations would prevail. With this ideal in mind, he inaugurated the summer school at Trois Pistoles in 1933. These classes, which have continued from year to year, have given wonderful results in the field of good relations.
We have among us here in parliament a former pupil of the school who attended
The Budget-Mr. Rousseau classes in 1935-1936. He did not speak French when he first came to Trois Pistoles, but he learned to express himself fluently in that language which now, fifteen years later, he still speaks very well. I refer to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) who is still an eligible bachelor.
This school is directed by Dr. H. E. Jenkins, one of the professors attached to Western university in London. In recognition of his admirable and patriotic work in the sphere of education, Quebec's Laval university conferred on him an honorary doctorate.
May I add, Mr. Speaker, that the university authorities were kind enough to come to Trois Pistoles in order to confer this honorary degree upon this distinguished gentleman, an unprecedented event in the history of the university. The generosity of a Catholic university towards a gentleman of another faith is a fine example of the friendly relations which exist between these races, without religious or racial distinction.
I cannot help but tell you and I am proud so to proclaim: the generosity of Western university towards Monsignor Vandry, rector of Laval university of Quebec, and towards one of my distinguished fellow citizens of Trois Pistoles, chief inspector Epiphane L'ltalien, was equal to that of Laval, since that institution conferred the handsome degree of Doctor of Laws honoris causa on those two gentlemen.
Just recently Western university did itself proud by writing on its honour roll the name of another distinguished doctor of laws, that of the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent).
In so doing, I know that the authorities of Western university have wished to grant recognition to the great administrative qualities and more particularly to the great legal mind of the Prime Minister of Canada, thus confirming and underlining the judgment passed more than thirty years ago by the Prime Minister's former employer.
Pleasant things were said on that occasion. The Prime Minister was so kind as to speak of Trois Pistoles, my native town. I thank him most sincerely for that.
If the Liberal government were to grant a few thousand dollars as an encouragement to these summer courses, taking care however not to infringe upon the educational rights of the provinces, they could not make a more patriotic gesture. The Carnegie Institute of

The Budget-Mr. Rousseau New York has been granting, these last three years, substantial sums to encourage these summer courses. That generous gesture was not interpreted as an infringement upon the rights of the provinces.
The lumber trade adds to the importance of Trois Pistoles. It is the most important dressed lumber exporting port in the eastern part of the province and even in the eastern part of the country. Each year, more than 125 million feet of lumber are dressed there, part of the lumber being sent in transit from the maritimes either by rail or water.
The service given by the C.N.R. is good, but the wharf needs to be extended and improved in order that the schooners and other coasting vessels coming from the north shore may load and unload. I am grateful to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) who favoured us with a visit three years ago in order to see for himself the work which had to be done, 'and I thank him for what he gave us. However I would like to suggest to him that he should not stop there; I know that he will pay attention to my request and grant us that which is part of the war effort of this country.
For the last fifty years there has been a daily steamship service between Trois Pistoles and Les Escoumains. The ship starts to operate when the ice is still in the river, on April 15, and stops when the river is freezing over, on November 15. That steamship service is very valuable to the parishes on each side, both for mail and passenger transport.
In the spring when the trains cannot get through on the north shore because of the swollen rivers, the mail which is delivered by land is often two or three days late. The ship from Trois Pistoles picks up the mail from Quebec, Montreal and Toronto at 4.30 a.m. and delivers it at Les Escoumains, for Baie Comeau. Thanks to the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) and to my hon. colleagues from Gaspe and Saguenay, this service has been renewed this year and I sincerely thank those hon. gentlemen.
Now, last but not least, we come to Rimouski. Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the great disaster which befell this beautiful and prosperous little town last year. Fire, that great destroyer, caused several million dollars worth of damage, and the people of the county seat have not yet recovered from the effects of this catastrophe. I know the government has been generous. I even know that the kind-hearted Prime Minister went to the scene of the fire to see the damage for

himself, and the plight of these good people. I thank him for what has already been done and again I convey to him the thanks of all the poor victims of that disaster. I understand that the need is still great and urgent, but I know that the government will not turn a deaf ear to the requests I may be asked to make.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to general politics. I am aware that Canada, like other democratic countries, is faced with a most distressing problem.
I feel that the United Nations' decision to keep a well equipped army on a war footing in Europe under the able leadership of General Eisenhower, the greatest general and strategist of modern times, and of his assistant Field Marshal Montgomery, is bound to reassure us in regard to the actual threat of war, and when the Prime Minister tells us he believes and still hopes that war is avoidable, he does so not only to reassure the people, but because he has good reasons to think so.
We must truly place our confidence in the government. The members of the cabinet have shown, in the past, that they have the interest of the Canadian people at heart. The Canadian people have confidence in the government which they returned to power two years ago. As far as I am concerned, as the representative of 30,000 electors, I have complete trust in the straightforwardness, honesty and competence of those who make up our government. That is why, during my electoral campaign, I stated I was a Liberal, I accepted and endorsed the Liberal party's actions, the party in which I had put all my trust. As such, Mr. Speaker, I was elected and as such I have voted for the government. This was indeed the mandate I received from my electors and I wish to remain true to it.
I am not surprised at the government's reticence as regards steps to be taken for the defence of our country and as a member of the United Nations. At the beginning of the second great war, I was in the office of the late Hon. Ernest Lapointe. As he seemed tired, I asked him what was worrying him. He replied: "If the people knew what news comes to us ministers, every twenty-four hours from England, France, Belgium, they would be desperate". Today, the situation is less critical. We should therefore have confidence in those we have honoured with our trust.

I know, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members, like myself, have received from their electors letters about the high cost of living, requesting the establishment of price controls. Again, Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the members of the government are aware of the situation and will make the necessary decisions at the proper time.
In closing, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Richard) on his interesting speech and especially on the part dealing with his visit to Rome last year.
He suggested that Canada send a representative to the Vatican.
I heartily support the hon. member's motion. I do so not as a Catholic but because the Pope, whose reign is so glorious, is considered by every right-thinking nation as one of the greatest diplomats of modern times.
One of the most famous and renowned of American presidents, the late Franklin D. Roosevelt, who, at the request of his people, served during four consecutive terms-something unique in American history-was not a Catholic. Yet, every month, from the beginning to the end of the war, his confidential representative, Mr. Myron Taylor, a non-Catholic, was sent to call on the Pope and ask his advice.
In these critical times we need the advice of wise and impartial persons. His Holiness Pope Pius XII is one of the wisest men on earth.
It is therefore proper and reasonable that he be consulted. I will therefore support
The Budget-Mr. Rousseau the resolution for the appointment of a Canadian representative to the Vatican.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that I will do as I have done since I came to this house and will support the government on the budget issue.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for his ability in securing acceptance of an operation that could have been more painful than it turned out to be. With his usual smile, he reminds me of a dentist who is sure to hurt his patients, but who knows how to divert their attention with fine words.
Nevertheless I will make so bold as to suggest to him that he modify that part of the budget which concerns the increased tax on refrigerators, electric stoves and washing machines, which are absolutely essential domestic appliances. To compensate that increase, he should raise the tax on alcoholic beverages.
This tax would increase our revenues and would help to prevent much criticism. In so doing the minister would please an immense number of housekeepers who would be eternally grateful to him for having taken that step.
